question: How flat does the floor have to be for large-format tile?
title: How Flat Must a Floor Be for Large-Format Tile?
h1: How Flat Does Your Subfloor Need to Be for Large-Format Tile?
description: Large-format tile needs a substrate flat within 1/8 in over 10 ft per ANSI A108.02; self-leveling to fix a Sarasota slab runs $3-$9/sq ft in 2026.
capsule: Large-format tile, meaning any edge 15 inches or longer, needs a substrate flat within 1/8 inch over 10 feet and 1/16 inch over 24 inches, per ANSI A108.02. Most Sarasota and Manatee County slabs need self-leveling underlayment to meet that standard, which typically runs $3-$9 per sq ft installed in 2026.

sections.html: ANSI defines large-format tile as anything with at least one edge 15 in. or longer - that covers most of the 24x24 in. and 24x48 in. porcelain planks that have become the default choice in new Sarasota and Lakewood Ranch construction, along with big rectified subway-style tile used on backsplashes and shower walls. Bigger tile means fewer grout lines to hide an uneven floor, which is exactly why the flatness standard is stricter for it than for a standard 12x12 in. tile. It's part of why we treat tile installation quotes for large-format product as a different job than a standard-tile quote, even in the same room.

sections.h2: How flat does the substrate actually have to be
sections.html:
ANSI A108.02 sets the tolerance at no more than 1/8 in. of variation over any 10-ft span, and no more than 1/16 in. over any 24-in. span, for substrates receiving tile with a long edge of 15 in. or more. Once the tile is set, allowable lippage - the height difference where two tile edges meet - is 1/32 in. with a grout joint of 1/16 in. or less, and that number has to account for any warpage in the tile itself, not just the installer's work.

A standard 12x12 in. tile is more forgiving of small dips and humps because the grout lines break up the sightline every foot. A 24x48 in. plank set over the same uneven slab will show every low spot as a visible rock or a lippage edge you can feel with a bare foot. This is the same underlying substrate check we run before any hardwood or vinyl job, just held to a tighter tolerance because tile doesn't flex the way a floating floor can.

sections.h2: Why this trips up older Florida slabs
sections.html: A slab poured in the 1970s or 1980s for a standard-format tile or terrazzo finish was rarely finished to today's large-format tolerance, and additions or patched sections often sit at a slightly different height than the original pour. We check flatness with a straightedge and feeler gauge during the estimate, before quoting a large-format job, because a slab that's fine for 12x12 in. tile can still fail the tighter large-format standard. A house that's had a slab-on-grade addition tacked onto an original 1970s footprint is one of the more common flatness failures we find, since the two pours were never intended to sit at exactly the same elevation.

A 50 lb bag of self-leveler covers roughly 50 sq ft at 1/8 in. thick, or only 12-15 sq ft at 1/2 in. - so a slab with deep low spots costs more to level than one that's just slightly out of tolerance. We build that into the written estimate as its own line item, separate from the tile and labor, so you can see exactly what the leveling step is adding to the job. Read more about the process on our subfloor leveling page, or start with a free estimate and we'll test your slab before quoting large-format tile.

One more scheduling detail worth knowing: leveling compound needs to cure before thinset goes on top of it, so budget an extra day beyond the tile-setting time itself. Skipping that cure time to save a day is a common shortcut, and it tends to show up later as tile that never fully bonded to the substrate underneath - the same hollow-sounding tile problem a flat, properly cured slab is supposed to prevent in the first place.

faqs.q: Can I skip self-leveling if my floor looks flat to the eye?
faqs.a: No. A 1/4 in. dip over 10 ft is often invisible to the eye but well outside the ANSI A108.02 tolerance for large-format tile, and it will show up as lippage once the tile is down.

faqs.q: Does self-leveling add much time to a tile job?
faqs.a: Usually one extra day for the compound to cure before tile-setting starts, since most self-levelers need to fully dry before thinset will bond to them.

faqs.q: Is large-format tile a bad choice if my slab is uneven?
faqs.a: Not necessarily - it just means the leveling step isn't optional. A smaller-format tile can sometimes avoid that cost, but large-format's clean, fewer-grout-line look is popular enough that most customers choose to level rather than downsize the tile.
